query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small concentration (0.1–0.5 at.%) of boron during alloy fabrication will lead to boron segregation at the lamellar colony boundaries in eutectic high-entropy alloys, promoting the formation of fine intergranular boride precipitates. This modification is expected to enhance grain boundary cohesion, thereby improving both the tensile strength and room-temperature ductility relative to the unmodified alloy, which typically fails by microcrack-induced intergranular fracture.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies characterized by numerous internal boundaries that are prone to microcracking under room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Introduce 0.1–0.5 at.% boron during alloy fabrication followed by appropriate heat treatment to allow boron to segregate to the lamellar boundaries.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile loading on eutectic HEAs with dual-phase lamellar colonies; processing conditions that permit controlled boron segregation without forming excessive brittle phases.
generation.structural_mediator: Fine intergranular boride precipitates formed along the lamellar boundaries which increase local hardness and cohesion.
generation.mechanism: During solidification and subsequent heat treatment, the minor added boron preferentially gathers at the lamellar colony boundaries, where it forms fine boride precipitates. These precipitates strengthen grain boundary regions by impeding crack initiation and propagation, reducing microcracking, and aiding in a more homogeneous stress distribution. In turn, the improved boundary strength contributes to work hardening under tensile load, thereby enhancing both strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified alloy, the boron-doped alloy will exhibit increased ultimate tensile strength and greater tensile ductility, with a shift in fracture mode from predominantly intergranular to more transgranular failure due to improved boundary cohesion.
generation.baseline: Unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloys suffer from grain boundary brittleness and early microcracking, leading to limited tensile ductility and strength.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected under controlled boron addition (0.1–0.5 at.%), in alloys where the lamellar colony boundaries can effectively accommodate boron segregation. Deviations in boron concentration or processing parameters that lead to excessive or insufficient precipitation may not yield the anticipated improvements.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of strength and ductility improvements remains uncertain and will likely depend on the exact boron content and processing conditions. Further tuning is required to optimize the beneficial effects without triggering unwanted brittle phases.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples: one set fabricated without boron (baseline) and one set with 0.1–0.5 at.% boron addition. Subject both sets to identical heat treatment and processing protocols. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests alongside detailed microstructural analyses (using TEM/SEM) to verify boron segregation and the formation of intergranular borides.
measurements: Tensile stress–strain curves to evaluate yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility
High-resolution microscopy (TEM/SEM) to identify boride precipitates at the colony boundaries
Fractography to assess crack initiation sites and fracture modes
Hardness tests localized at grain boundaries versus the matrix
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in both ultimate tensile strength and ductility relative to the baseline, or if microstructural analysis fails to reveal the expected boride formation and enhanced boundary cohesion, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractTo develop strong refractory high-entropy alloys for use at elevated temperatures as well as to overcome grain-boundary brittleness, an equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was prepared, and a minor amount of boron (0.1 at.%) was added into the alloy. The microstructures of the alloys were characterized, and their macro-to-microscale mechanical properties were measured. The microstructural observations indicated that the matrices of both the alloys were composed of a body-centered cubic solid-solution structure, and the added boron induced the precipitation of hexagonal close-packed borides (most likely the (Hf, Zr)B2) at the grain boundaries. The modulus and hardness of differently oriented grains were about equivalent, suggesting a diminished anisotropy, and many small slips occurred on multiple {110} planes. While the hardness of the matrix was not increased, the intergranular precipitation of the borides markedly raised the hardness of the grain boundaries. Owing to the enhanced grain boundary cohesion, the work hardenability and ductility were effectively improved with the addition of boron.Keywords: refractory alloy, high-entropy alloy, boride, grain boundary, mechanical prop
